definition: Computational linguistics is an interdisciplinary field concerned with the computational modelling of natural language, as well as the study of appropriate computational approaches to linguistic questions.
details: In general, computational linguistics draws upon linguistics, computer science, artificial intelligence, mathematics, logic, philosophy, cognitive science, cognitive psychology, psycholinguistics, anthropology and neuroscience, among others. Computational linguistics is closely related to mathematical linguistics.

explainer.lead: Computational linguistics connects the scientific study of language with computational modelling. It matters because the same models can help researchers investigate linguistic questions and help software work with speech or text.

tiers.eli5: Language is like a game whose rules we usually follow without noticing them. Computational linguistics tries to describe those rules clearly enough for a computer to work with them, while also using computers to learn more about how people use language.
tiers.practitioner: A practitioner represents linguistic structure in data, chooses a computational model, and evaluates its output against a defined language task or research question. Work can draw on linguistics, computer science, mathematics, logic, and cognitive disciplines. Common pitfalls include mistaking fluent output for linguistic understanding and letting modelling assumptions hide ambiguity or variation in natural language.
tiers.paperLevel: Computational linguistics is the computational modelling of natural language and the study of computational approaches to linguistic questions. A typical formulation maps language data to formal representations or predictions through a model whose linguistic and mathematical assumptions can be examined. Its conclusions are constrained by those assumptions and by the available linguistic evidence.

explainer.example: For the sentence “The chicken is ready to eat,” a model might represent two interpretations: the chicken is prepared to eat something, or the chicken is prepared as food. Comparing computational representations of these readings helps make the sentence’s ambiguity explicit.

explainer.intuition: Natural language is systematic but ambiguous, so working with it requires both linguistic knowledge and explicit computational models. The field uses each to strengthen the other: linguistics informs models, and models provide ways to investigate language.
howItWorks: Start with a linguistic question or a language-processing task.
Choose representations for relevant properties of the language data.
Build a computational model using appropriate linguistic and mathematical assumptions.
Apply the model and examine its representations, analyses, or predictions.
Evaluate the results and revise the representations or model.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a shared framework for studying language scientifically and building systems that process it. Its interdisciplinary approach links formal modelling with evidence about human language and cognition.
misconceptions: It is not simply counting words; it concerns computational models of natural language.
It does not replace linguistics with computer science, but draws on both and on several related disciplines.
